q: how to get rid of garden pests naturally
how to keep bugs off my vegetable garden
how to get rid of aphids
how to deal with garden pests without pesticides
a: Natural pest control starts with prevention and works up from there. (1) Healthy plants resist pests — right soil, water, and spacing; stressed plants attract bugs. (2) Encourage predators: ladybugs and lacewings eat aphids; birds, frogs, and beneficial wasps eat caterpillars. Plant flowers like dill, yarrow, and marigolds to attract them — 'companion planting' (marigolds near tomatoes, basil near peppers) helps. (3) Physical barriers: floating row covers keep insects off young plants; hand-picking caterpillars and beetles (drop in soapy water) works for small gardens. (4) For soft-bodied pests like aphids and mites: a strong spray of water knocks them off, or spray a mix of a few drops of dish soap per liter of water (reapply every few days); neem oil is an effective natural pesticide for many pests — apply in the evening so you don't harm bees. (5) Diatomaceous earth dusts around stems and on leaves to deter crawling insects. (6) Slug control: beer traps or copper tape around beds; hand-pick at dusk. (7) Rotate crops yearly and clean up dead plant material where pests overwinter. Chemical pesticides are a last resort — they kill the beneficial insects that were protecting you, which is why infestations often come back worse after spraying.

q: how to grow tomatoes from seed
how to care for tomato plants
a: Tomatoes are warm-season plants: start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost (or buy seedlings), and transplant only when night temperatures stay above 10°C (50°F) — cold kills them. Give them the three things they need: (1) Sun — a full 6-8 hours of direct sunlight; more sun = more fruit. (2) Support — stake, cage, or trellis them at planting time; sprawling plants rot and get diseases. (3) Water — deep, consistent watering at the base (not on the leaves, which spreads blight), about 2.5 cm (1 inch) per week; erratic watering causes blossom-end rot (the black bottoms) and cracked fruit. Pinch off the suckers (shoots in the leaf joints) for indeterminate varieties to keep plants manageable. Feed every 2-3 weeks with a tomato/balanced fertilizer once flowers appear. Harvest when fully colored and slightly soft; tomatoes ripen off the vine fine if frost threatens (pick green ones, ripen on a windowsill). Big mistakes: planting too early, over-fertilizing with nitrogen (huge plants, no fruit), and inconsistent watering. Cherry tomatoes are the easiest; big beefsteaks need the most patience.

q: how to water plants while on vacation
how to keep plants alive while away
how to water plants when on holiday
a: Before you leave: move plants out of direct sun into a cooler, shadier room — less light means less water demand (this alone doubles how long they last). Water everything thoroughly the day before you go, and group plants together so they share humidity. Then pick a method by trip length: (1) A few days: the bath-tub method works — put a towel in the tub, lay plants on it, fill the tub with a few cm of water; the towel wicks moisture up to the pots (don't leave it deeper than the pot base). (2) Up to a week: DIY wick — fill a bottle/jug with water, put one end of a cotton string or shoelace in the water and the other end in the soil; capillary action drips slowly. The classic: the wine-bottle trick — fill a bottle with water, invert it into the soil. (3) For houseplants specifically: self-watering spikes (ceramic or plastic cones that screw onto bottles) work for most pots. (4) Long trips or many plants: a timer drip system (Blumat or a simple timer + drip line) or ask a neighbor — honestly, the neighbor or house-sitter is the most reliable option, with written instructions per plant. Cacti and succulents need nothing — leave them alone.
